title: Deviations, Root-Cause Analysis, and CAPA
requiredTeachingVisual: Deviation containment, investigation, CAPA, and effectiveness workflow
objective: Control departures from requirements through containment, evidence preservation, impact assessment, root-cause analysis, corrective action, and effectiveness verification.
coreScience: A deviation is a departure from an approved requirement, method, range, identity, process, or record. First protect people, crop, samples, equipment, and data. Containment can include stopping work, isolating material, preserving logs, marking affected units, securing samples, and preventing further processing. A correction restores an immediate condition; it is not automatically a corrective action that prevents recurrence.

Investigation should reconstruct the event timeline and define the problem precisely: what requirement applied, what occurred, when, where, to which units, for how long, and with what evidence. Review equipment, environment, materials, methods, training, workload, design, software, and prior events. “Operator error” is usually incomplete unless the system explains why the error was possible, undetected, or repeated. Five Whys, fishbone diagrams, fault trees, and change analysis organize questions but do not prove cause.

CAPA should address verified or strongly supported causes, assign owners and dates, control unintended consequences, update affected documents and training, and define measurable effectiveness checks. More testing can add evidence but cannot always prove an unsampled batch was unaffected. Closure requires authorized disposition of material and data, completion of actions, and evidence that recurrence risk was reduced.
cultivationRelevance: Use a single controlled deviation record linked to affected plants, batches, instruments, files, samples, SOP versions, and release decisions.
measureAndRecord: Assign a deviation ID and record the applicable requirement and version, event date and time, location, affected entities, reporter, immediate safety or containment action, and preserved raw evidence.

Build a timeline and assess impact, uncertainty, extent, and potential recurrence before assigning causes. Distinguish direct cause, contributing factors, systemic conditions, and unsupported assumptions.
Record correction, corrective and preventive actions, owner, due date, linked change control, effectiveness metric, verification date, residual risk, disposition, approver, and closure evidence.
misconceptions: Passing a retest automatically invalidates the original failure. A retest is additional evidence and does not erase the need to explain the original result and determine whether the retest was justified.
Root cause is always one person or one failed component. Complex failures can arise from interacting process, equipment, training, environment, design, and management factors.
Completing the action item proves the CAPA was effective. Effectiveness requires evidence that recurrence risk or the targeted process measure actually improved after implementation.
evidenceLimits: Root-cause certainty can remain incomplete even after a careful investigation; decisions should state evidence strength, uncertainty, residual risk, and authority.
CAPA systems can improve control but cannot guarantee zero recurrence, especially when underlying mechanisms are only partially understood.

knowledgeCheck: For "Deviations, Root-Cause Analysis, and CAPA", explain the mechanism behind this objective: Control departures from requirements through containment, evidence preservation, impact assessment, root-cause analysis, corrective action, and effectiveness verification. Which observation or measurement would best test whether that mechanism is operating in the real crop?

A learner claims, "Completing the action item proves the CAPA was effective." Use the lesson's science and evidence limits to explain why that claim is unreliable, then identify the effectiveness evidence and follow-up interval needed before closure.

Applied case — Use a single controlled deviation record linked to affected plants, batches, instruments, files, samples, SOP versions, and release decisions. Build a verification plan using the lesson's record set (Deviation ID; requirement and version; event date/time/location; reporter; affected entities; immediate safety/containment; raw evidence; timeline; impact and uncertainty; causes and evidence; correction; CAPA owner/due date; change control; effectiveness metric/date; disposition/approver; closure.). What would you compare before and after the action, and what result would make you revise the original interpretation?
